item.title: Steam Deck docked as a TV console finally works, and it's just one setting away
item.itunes:title: Steam Deck docked as a TV console finally works, and it's just one setting away
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When looking for a family game console, you might opt for a PS5 or Xbox Series X, which is great for high-end single-player epics. This traditional console market has seemingly abandoned the golden era of local couch co-op, party games, and accessible retro titles, though the Nintendo Switch has filled the gap somewhat. Rebuying multi-platform games at $60 a pop, plus paying for annual online passes, stings.

I've got a massive Steam library, which I've accumulated over the past decade, including hundreds of local multiplayer indie titles, and I've also got a Steam Deck. With a $30 USB-C dock, I was able to plug it into my TV, pair a load of controllers, and suddenly my living room entertainment was solved. But it wasn't as easy as I first thought. When I booted up a game, Player 1 was assigned to the Steam Deck's built-in physical buttons. At the same time, the TV renders an ugly, blurry 720p image stretched across 4K, or the APU melts trying to render native 4K. Some settings are fundamental when you're trying to use your gaming handheld as a family console.

4 reasons a Steam Deck shouldn’t replace your dedicated gaming PC

We're evaluating why Valve's Steam Deck isn't a worthwhile replacement for a dedicated gaming PC

2
By  Andre Revilla

When docking a Steam Deck, there are some issues

But these can be resolved

Docking a handheld isn't as easy as plugging in a console. Some architectural friction points exist between handheld Linux gaming and a fixed 4K TV setup.

The first is the controller order priority issue. In handheld mode, the Deck's integrated controller is permanently hard-coded as device 1. This means that when you dock the Deck and pair external Bluetooth or 2.4 GHz dongle controllers (whether that's a DualSense or Xbox wireless controller or a third-party edition), legacy games using X input or raw SDL input mapping bind Player 1 strictly to the first enumerated device. As a result, the physical handheld in the media console gets Player 1, while everyone on the couch is stuck as Player 2 or 3, or ignored entirely.

Another major issue is the resolution mismatch. The Steam Deck is an 800p device, so playing on a 4K TV results in a stretched, not-so-pleasant-to-look-at display. When you output to a 4K panel over HDMI 2.0 or 2.1, the TV receives an 800p image scaled up by basic linear filtering, resulting in soft, muddy text and vaseline-smeared textures.

Conversely, setting the Dex global display output to 4K forces unoptimized games to attempt native 3840 x 2160 rendering, bringing the 15W APU to a slideshow crawl. You're essentially melting your device from the inside.

How to fix these issues

With a few tweaks, you can rectify these problems

What setting can fix the experience? There are software toggles and mechanics that bring appliance-like polish to a Steam Deck. The core fix is the per-game display resolution override and FSR auto-scale.

You can sort this out by navigating to Game Properties, then General, then Game Resolution, and then set to 900 x 1080 and check "Set resolution for internal and external display."

The reason this setting changes everything is that the rendering target is set cleanly to 1080p, allowing the game engine to render assets, HUDs, and split-screen viewports at crisp full HD resolution. It also unlocks SteamOS-level FSR, meaning the Deck renders at 1080p and uses hardware-accelerated spatial upscaling to output a pristine, razor-sharp 4K signal to the TV without choking the GPU. You still get that crisp, sharp 4K display on the TV itself.

There's also a setting you might benefit from: "Automatic Controller Reordering." You can permanently reorder the controller stack in the Quick Access menu by hitting the ellipses button or guide button. That way, external wireless controllers automatically inherit player 1 through 4 priority over the built-in chassis inputs whenever a dock connection is detected.

What hardware should you invest in?

Getting the right dock is fundamental

When choosing hardware to dock your Steam Deck, it's essential to pick the right kit. When choosing a dock, you should pick one with an Ethernet port and HDMI 2.0 so that you get 4K at 60Hz output. Also, upgrading from the stock 45W charger to a 65W USB Power Delivery brick can handle docking power draw, external dongles, and fast battery charging simultaneously without discharging under heavy load.

When it comes to controllers, you can mix and match what you already own. You can pair PS4 or PS5 DualSense controllers, Xbox wireless controllers over native Bluetooth, and pretty much any third-party controller that connects via 2.4GHz, as long as you have USB ports on your dock or Bluetooth. Steam Input normalizes button layouts, translating Nintendo face-button placement to an Xbox layout, so guests never get confused by on-screen prompts.

Enjoy your Steam Deck on the big screen too

Don't be restricted

The dedicated home console is being increasingly worn down by subscription paywalls, closed ecosystems, and digital purchases that don't carry over between generations. The Steam Deck proves that PC gaming's greatest strength (its open library and infinite backward compatibility) can comfortably live under the TV. Don't let your Steam Deck sit in a drawer collecting dust whenever you're not traveling. Drop it into an inexpensive dock, tweak your resolution overrides, pair your controllers, and enjoy the most versatile family gaming console you already own.

item.title: I turned my 7-year-old Kindle Fire into a second monitor, and it’s useful again
item.itunes:title: I turned my 7-year-old Kindle Fire into a second monitor, and it’s useful again
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When Amazon first announced the Kindle Fire tablet line, I was curious to see how a cheap tablet would fare against the iPad. Needless to say, it didn't. Still, I gave the 13th-gen Fire HD 10 a second chance when it was released. Not much is happening with it either, and for seven years it has been collecting dust. I had actually forgotten about it.

I found the tablet in my hoard of devices and thought I would see if I could turn it into something useful, like a second monitor for my Windows laptop. My journey took some twists and turns, but I finally landed on the best way to make it a tangible option.

Building a second monitor

Getting my old Kindle Fire Tablet ready for duty

You can't simply plug the Kindle Fire HD 10 into a PC with an HDMI-to-USB-A or USB-C cable without extra software. Several apps can do this, like DuetDisplay, SuperDisplay, or Deskreen. After some research, I went with Spacedesk to connect the tablet wirelessly. But to start, the tablet hadn't held a charge in years, so I dug out the old charging cable and plugged it in. It took a full day to charge, but I wanted it fully charged since I didn't know how things would go.

I realized the data and settings on the Fire HD were old, and I wanted a fresh start, so I reset it to factory settings. I didn't want anything to conflict with the software I was installing. I also enabled developer settings and allowed apps from unknown sources, not because I needed to for this specific project, but because I always do on Android-based devices.

6 cool projects to reuse your old monitor

Old displays still have a lot of life in them, even if the backlight is gone.

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Getting software together

Apps and settings need adjusting

I started by installing Spacedesk Driver on my Windows machine since it's the go-to software for most of the Fire HD owners I spoke to. The software is also available for macOS, so you can try this with a Fire HD and your Mac. Installation is straightforward; just allow it through the Windows Firewall when prompted.

Once that is installed and running, the next thing I needed to do was install the Spacedesk Viewer app on my Fire HD tablet. I found it in the Amazon Appstore under the name "Spacedesk Display Screen Cast." It's simply called Spacedesk in the Google Play Store, but it's the same app. If I wanted to be picky about a name or version number, I could have sideloaded the Spacedesk Viewer APK, but I just needed it to work so I could have my second monitor.

I made sure Spacedesk Driver was running on my machine. The console offers several options when it's open, from requiring a password and encryption to running diagnostics, clearing Windows display settings, exporting Spacedesk settings, and more. I launched the app on the Fire HD 10, and it recognized the two computers where I'd installed the Spacedesk Driver app. I tapped my laptop, and it connected in seconds.

Using the Fire Tablet as a monitor

Physical placement and tying up loose ends

Once it was connected, there was very little lag, but viewing a complete Windows desktop on such a small display isn't feasible. A 10-inch screen can make things hard to see, so I went into Windows Display settings, found the tablet acting as a monitor, and changed the resolution and bumped the scaling to 150%, since anything higher was too much. I also locked the tablet in landscape mode, so the virtual screen doesn't rotate unexpectedly. Now I have a second monitor, and I can control the desktop with a tap or a swipe.

Spacedesk Viewer
See at Amazon See at Google

​​​​​​​

My newly repurposed Fire tablet was working as I had hoped. The next obstacle was finding the right placement of the Fire HD tablet next to my monitor. I used to have a stand designed specifically for the Fire HD 10. It let me turn the tablet into an Echo-like device I could place in the kitchen or another room for easy access. Since I no longer have it (or can't find it anyway), I used a small picture frame to prop it up next to my laptop screen on my desk.

Since I usually use my laptop at home with the Fire HD as a second monitor, on the same network and close to my router, I find a wireless connection easiest. I am not a fan of dealing with wires if I don't have to. However, you can also hardwire them with a USB cable. This is a good reason to enable Developer Options, which are required along with USB debugging on the Fire tablet when using a physical connection.

I gave my old Android tablet a second life as a wireless Android Auto screen, and my car radio hasn't been touched since

Open Headunit transformed my dashboard with a tablet-sized Android Auto screen that cost me nothing

9
By  Dhruv Bhutani

A handy use for an old device

Overall, I am glad I thought about bringing the Kindle Fire HD tablet back from the dead. It really makes a great second monitor when I use my laptop. I keep my main work on the laptop's main display and put media playing in VLC or an open email inbox on the Fire's screen. Spacedesk does a good job, and if I ever need to hardwire the screens together, I can — with different settings.

item.title: 6 Docker containers helped me reduce dependency on Google eco-system
item.itunes:title: 6 Docker containers helped me reduce dependency on Google eco-system
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Google has become the default for almost everything online. I used to open a Google service without thinking about it, whether I needed to store something, check a schedule, or manage everyday information. Over time, though, I started wondering how much of my digital life actually needed to depend on one ecosystem.

Since I already run Docker on my own hardware, I began looking for practical self-hosted alternatives. I wasn't looking for complicated projects or perfect replacements. I wanted tools that could handle specific jobs well and fit into my existing workflow. These are six Docker containers that helped me gradually build a more independent setup.

Immich

A Google Photos alternative I actually use

Immich was one of the first containers I tried when I wanted to move more of my personal data away from Google. I use it as my own photo library, and the experience feels surprisingly close to what I was used to with Google Photos.

What I like most is how quickly I can find older pictures. My photos are organized into a timeline, and Immich gives me useful search and organization features without making the interface feel complicated. item.itunes:title: Your CPU has been thermally throttled since day one, and one BIOS setting fixes it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Everyone wants to squeeze more performance out of their hardware. Whether it's a CPU or GPU, there's something deeply satisfying about getting more out of the hardware you already own. The problem is that performance rarely comes without a cost. If you push a component harder, you usually end up with more power consumption, and in turn, more heat, and when it comes to chips, it imposes a limit to how far you can push them.

I've spent the past few days experimenting with my Ryzen 7000 series chip to see if I could break that trade off, and to find if I could get more performance without turning the rig into more of a space heater than it already is. As it turns out, there is a way, and the solution was quite literally just a BIOS toggle.

Precision Boost Overdrive gave my Ryzen chip more power it couldn't use

20W of headroom my 7600X couldn't touch

AMD and board manufacturers love to sell Precision Boost Overdrive (PBO) as the one toggle that unlocks free performance, and most "one-click OC" and "Game Mode" presets that you see in your BIOS are just PBO in disguise. What they fail to tell you is that PBO only helps a chip that has thermal headroom to grow into. On a chip that already runs close to the ceiling at stock, raising the power limit changes very little except the temperature.

Likewise, my Ryzen 5 7600X never disappointed when it came to performance, but its thermal behavior has been the first thing I'd want to change. At stock settings, my two multithreaded runs on Cinebench 2026 averaged 122.7W of package power and 94.7°C Tdie, putting the CPU right up against its thermal ceiling.

What's even more disappointing is the fact that it wasn't using all the power available to it. The 7600X has a 142W default package power limit, and yet my runs averaged at 122.7W and peaked at 132.8W before being reined back in. The chip kept reaching for more power and kept hitting TjMax, which meant it was hitting its thermal limit every time.

This is exactly why simply enabling PBO does little for a chip in this state. PBO raises power and current limits, but a CPU already grazing TjMax with watts to spare has no way of actually leveraging the headroom. The solution, therefore, became as simple as it could be in this case. I was looking for a lever that lowers the temperature at the same clock.

I lowered my CPU temps by 15 degrees without spending a single dollar

I dropped my Ryzen temps by about 15°C with zero spend — just smart tweaks.

By  Samarveer Singh

The real problem was the curve AMD ships every chip on

One voltage table for a million dies

AMD and other chip manufacturers have to make their voltage-frequency curve work across a range of individual chips, even though no two pieces of silicon have the same voltage or thermal characteristics. My 7600X doesn't necessarily need the same amount of voltage as another 7600X to reach a given clock speed, but the processor starts working for a common curve designed to accommodate that variation.

This is a simple problem with a simple solution, and the BIOS toggle you'd be looking at to fix the issue is the Curve Optimizer. Curve Optimizer lets one adjust the curve without manually locking the CPU to a frequency or voltage. A negative offset here tells the processor that it can target the same frequency at a lower voltage, thereby reducing power and heat required to reach those operating points. On a chip that's thermally bound, that frees up thermal headroom that finally lets the boost algorithm climb instead of throttle.

I undervolted my CPU and GPU at the same time, and my PC runs cooler, quieter, and just as fast

Undervolting is easier and more beneficial than ever

5
By  Abhinav Raj

Curve Optimizer made my Ryzen processor faster and cooler at once

And I logged every watt and degree to prove it

Of course, I wouldn't be claiming all of this if I didn't bring the benchmark numbers myself. I set the Precision Boost Overdrive to Enabled, and then dialed the Curve Optimizer to a negative 15 offset across all cores, and re-ran the same two Cinebench 2026 tests from before.

Multithreaded Test

Score

The multithreaded score climbed a little over 5% from a score of 3223 average to 3390. This is particularly interesting because, as you can see, the package power actually dropped, and Tdie barely moved, falling only 1.6°C. The chip was still pressed right against the thermal wall it hit at stock, but the lower voltage let it hold an average clock of about 157MHz higher across all six cores for the run.

What we're seeing here is the chip running faster at the same temperature, because the boost algorithm spent every degree the undervolt freed up.

In the single core test, the chip had thermal headroom to begin with, so the undervolt served a different purpose. The score rose about 3%, but the package power fell more than 8W and Tdie dropped a full 6°C. On the very same chip, same silicon. In this case, the savings from the Curve Optimizer configuration showed up as lower power and heat, while the peak boost clock still climbed by 173MHz.

I got more performance by giving my Ryzen less to work with

A Curve Optimizer offset finally achieved what PBO couldn't do alone by letting my Ryzen 7000 series chip more room to boost without feeding it more power which would trip it up. I was able to get a free 5.2% boost on multithreaded performance and 3.2% on single core performance while both power and temperatures fell, but believe it or not, this is actually only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to optimization via CO offsets, and depending on your chip, you might be able to unlock more performance on your processor than I did.

20W of headroom my 7600X couldn't touch

AMD and board manufacturers love to sell Precision Boost Overdrive (PBO) as the one toggle that unlocks free performance, and most "one-click OC" and "Game Mode" presets that you see in your BIOS are just PBO in disguise. What they fail to tell you is that PBO only helps a chip that has thermal headroom to grow into. On a chip that already runs close to the ceiling at stock, raising the power limit changes very little except the temperature.

Likewise, my Ryzen 5 7600X never disappointed when it came to performance, but its thermal behavior has been the first thing I'd want to change. At stock settings, my two multithreaded runs on Cinebench 2026 averaged 122.7W of package power and 94.7°C Tdie, putting the CPU right up against its thermal ceiling.

What's even more disappointing is the fact that it wasn't using all the power available to it. The 7600X has a 142W default package power limit, and yet my runs averaged at 122.7W and peaked at 132.8W before being reined back in. The chip kept reaching for more power and kept hitting TjMax, which meant it was hitting its thermal limit every time.

This is exactly why simply enabling PBO does little for a chip in this state. PBO raises power and current limits, but a CPU already grazing TjMax with watts to spare has no way of actually leveraging the headroom. The solution, therefore, became as simple as it could be in this case. I was looking for a lever that lowers the temperature at the same clock.

The real problem was the curve AMD ships every chip on

One voltage table for a million dies

AMD and other chip manufacturers have to make their voltage-frequency curve work across a range of individual chips, even though no two pieces of silicon have the same voltage or thermal characteristics. item.title: I gave my car a USB-C PD port for cheap, and it fixed my phone's battery problem
item.itunes:title: I gave my car a USB-C PD port for cheap, and it fixed my phone's battery problem
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I got my current car a couple of years ago, but it was already a fairly old model then, being from 2014. But it's the first car I've had that has a USB port, and when I first saw that, I figured I'd never have to worry about keeping my phone charged on trips again.

As it turned out, though, this port wasn't suitable for charging at all, but thankfully, it was easy to fix. Thanks to the 12V port on the car, I now have a USB-C charger in my car at all times, and it works exactly how I'd expect it to.

In-car USB ports are usually bad

Especially this early on

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

USB ports in cars can often be pretty bad, and that's only compounded when we're talking about something from 2014. The USB Type-A port in my car is basically completely incapable of charging a phone. It's only there to power the music player if I want to use local files, or to install software updates for the in-car display. The first time I got into the car for a long drive, I plugged in my phone for a long time, only to realize the battery was still draining pretty fast.

From talking with people who have more modern cars, I know they can charge better, but that doesn't mean they're great. XDA's Content Director Rich Woods even said he wouldn't buy a car unless the specs outlined the charging capabilities of the USB ports, because if manufacturers aren't mentioning it, there's a good chance it just charges too slowly, and if you're using Android Auto with your phone, it may end up not getting much of a charge at the end of the trip. That's where the 12V port inside my car came to the rescue.

A 12V adapter changed everything

Now everything charges as it should

For as long as I can remember, cars have come with a port that's prime for charging your phone. It's the 12V port, and though it was originally designed to power a small lighter built into the car, adapters have always turned that port into a phone charger. We used to call them "cigarette lighter chargers."

These days, it seems like these ports don't include the lighter anymore, but they're still just as good for charging, so that's what I did. I recently bought a kit that included both a phone holder and a 12V charging adapter, and that has solved all my woes.

Granted, this specific charger is actually still only rated for 15W out of the USB-C port (5V and 3A), but that's still a massive step up from not being charged at all, and on all my trips driving around, it always charges my phone faster than the battery drains from using Google Maps the whole time. I've never had to worry about my phone dying on one of these trips, even if I didn't charge it overnight.

Android Auto drains my phone faster than the car can charge it, and the fix wasn't a better cable

Android Auto drains faster than your car charges, but switching to the 12V socket changes everything

By  Dhruv Bhutani

Plus, you can definitely find more powerful chargers; I just went very cheap with this one, and I didn't even do any research. I just happened to find this at a store, so it's far from the best option out there. On Amazon, you can find the Anker 323 car charging adapter that can deliver up to 30W over a single USB-C port, and it still costs less than $20. It's a pretty sweet upgrade.

Of course, if you're also interested in using Android Auto, and it needs a wired connection, that may be a problem here. You can add wireless Android Auto with a dedicated adapter if you need it, though that will add a bit to your spending.

You could always go for an inverter

If you need more power

If you need even more power, there's one particular kind of adapter you can get. It's called an inverter, and it allows you to get way more power out of this simple 12V port. These devices usually give you proper outlets with even more wattage, so you can plug in a proper wall charger and juice up your phone or laptop much faster.

Admittedly, I haven't tried this, especially since these devices tend to be much more expensive, but if you want to charge multiple devices faster, that's probably the way to go. My colleague at XDA Dhruv Bhutani tried this, and it worked quite well for him.

A cheap adapter goes a long way

It was certainly disappointing to see the USB port in my car, only to later realize it wasn't useful for what I was most interested in, but fixing this problem is frankly very easy. Almost every car has a 12V port, and it's rarely used for anything else, so you might as well leave a cheap charger in there to make sure your phone can be fully charged during your trip.

Anker 323 compact car charger

This compact charging adapter for your car can output 30W out of its USB_C port, making it more than capable of charging any smartphone quickly.

$20 at Amazon

item.title: 3 household items I no longer buy from Amazon because 3D-printing them takes 40 minutes
item.itunes:title: 3 household items I no longer buy from Amazon because 3D-printing them takes 40 minutes
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
You know the drill. The first time you buy a 3D printer, it's understood that you'll be going down a rabbit hole of home accessories to print. But, as stereotypical as that might sound, there are plenty of small items that I just don't buy from Amazon anymore. These items aren't necessarily expensive, but printing out a replacement at home using my 3D printer is simply faster.

Lately, I've been using my 3D printer to solve small, annoying problems around my home, especially problems that can be easily solved with a simple piece of plastic and under an hour of free time. While there are dozens of such examples, and I'm sure I'm missing dozens more, here are three things that I printed just this week that solved daily frustrations.

8 unique 3D prints that I actually use every day

These are the genuinely useful 3D prints that I use the most in my home.

2
By  Adam Conway

Custom trays and organizers for my desk

Designing storage around my workspace

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

Every weekend I clear out my work desk, and by Monday, it is in bad shape already. My desk accumulates small pieces of tech faster than I can store them away. From adapters to memory cards, cables and other tidbits.

Conventional desk organizers can help, but most aren't really designed around my own desk setup. This means either wasted space or a shape and size that's too big or not very useful for my own space. I don't need multiple slots for pens, just two. USB storage, on the other hand, I need multiples of.

This is where printed trays and organizers come in handy. To begin with, I can design and print a tray that fits into a specific part of my desk instead of trying to find one with the dimensions that are best suited to my desk. If I have a narrow gap beside a monitor, for example, I can use that space instead of leaving it blank.

The same applies to compartments. I recently decided to dive into the Gridfinity bandwagon and printed out a full end-to-end grid for my two desk drawers. While I haven't printed out bins that fully occupy the space just yet, that's precisely the beauty of it. I can print as I go and shape the drawers for optimal space usage.

So far, I've got a bin with compartments to store hard drives, a bin with a lid for USB drives and a bin specifically designed to keep USB cables organized. That's better than anything I could ever just purchase off Amazon.

Print a bag clip or a dozen

A small print saves me a trip to the store

Bag clips are one of the first household items that made me realise how useful a 3D printer can be. It's something we always have a need for, and in a decent amount to boot. Look, I go through a lot of packets of snacks, coffee and cereal in the kitchen. My usual solution is to fold the packet over or use whatever clip I can find lying around. The problem with that is the former isn't particularly convenient. Folded bags have a tendency to pop open. Meanwhile, clips have a tendency to get lost. As it turns out, instead of buying more clips, I can just print them out.

The useful part here isn't that a 3D-printed clip is better than one I could just buy off Amazon. Instead, the convenience is in the fact that I can print one or a dozen out any time I want. These are small prints that use very little filament and don't take long to finish printing. Plus, I can print several at once any time I know I'm running low.

That's a huge upgrade over buying them from shops. For one, I don't have to wait for shipping every time I need an extra clip. Nor do I have to think about the cost or environmental impact of shipping something as basic as a single bag clip. Every time I need a spare, I end up printing a dozen and keep them around the kitchen. Every time one breaks or disappears, I just print another dozen. Simple.

Custom stands for headphones (and masks)

Height and size as I want them

Stands are another category where I just print out things instead of buying them anymore. The problem is pretty straightforward. I get a lot of headphones for testing, and there's no way I can keep enough stands just sitting around. Sure, I have a few, but any time I have more headphones than stands, I just print them out.

Similarly, I've got a collection of interesting masks. But any time I want to display them, I struggle to find a stand that's the right size. Some are too big, some too small. Others are not very aesthetic. So, I just print them out instead. I even got a lovely bronze-colored filament to give them a look that would fit perfectly in my decor.

It's easier to print the small stuff

Look, a 3D printer isn't going to replace every purchase. For example, I'm not going to print an oversized storage bin because the economics and time commitment of that just don't work out. But small, simple objects that solve specific problems are fair game in my books. I don't need to waste time waiting for an order to get delivered or rummage through drawers to find a bag clip. Printing it is just quicker, cheaper and a lot more fun. That's why, for a lot of these things, I just don't bother buying anymore.

Bambu Labs A2L

The Bambu A2L is a large-format bedslinger 3D printer capable of printing large volumes, and in multiple colors with AMS compatibility.

item.itunes:title: I moved my Claude Code prompts into skills files, and I'm slightly embarrassed by how much better it got
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most people who use AI tools tend to build up a stash of reusable prompts somewhere. Could be a Notion page, or a proper prompt library tool, or a little scratchpad sitting on your desktop that never gets closed. The specifics vary but the habit is essentially the same.

I never really questioned mine because it worked well. Then when I actually started moving the same prompts into Claude's skill files, the amount of manual routing I was doing became very clear, and there was no turning back…

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

Everyone has a prompt stash

Even if you don't call it one

A prompt library, officially, is a collection of reusable prompts you keep somewhere accessible so you don't have to retype them. In practice, if you use AI regularly, you probably already have one or some version of one - it might be a proper prompt tool like PromptLayer, or perhaps something you keep in a notepad, or perhaps something you just keep memorized.

Mine was predominantly sticky notes on my desktop. I'd adjust the prompts, but would keep reusable frameworks for my workflows in there, like scaffolding a low-fi wireframe with strict grayscale rules, or running a component critique against a specific checklist. It was a matter of remembering which one I needed, alt-tabbing to my notes, pasting it in, and adjusting it based on whatever the task was.

This is as barebones as it gets and works fine. But prompts often drift a lot when you tweak them in a session and forget to update the saved version, so next time pasting in the same prompt might not be applicable to the workflow anymore if it has evolved. You forget what you've even saved, so you occasionally re-solve something you already solved. And then there's also the fact that you have to do the routing yourself, scan your own stack, pick the right one, and manually handle it.

I borrowed Claude prompts from Anthropic engineers and immediately stopped wasting time on bad ones

The best prompts come from the team.

By  Mahnoor Faisal

Skills aren't prompts you save, they're instructions Claude picks up on its own

This difference is exactly where the improvement comes from

A skill in Claude Code is a folder. It lives at ~/.claude/skills/skill-name/ for your personal skills, or inside .claude/skills/ in a project if you want to share with a team. Inside is a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter (a name and a description) and the actual instructions in the body.

The bit that does the real work is auto-invocation. At startup, Claude Code loads only the name and description of every skill you have, roughly 100 tokens each. When you send a message, it checks whether any skill's description matches what you're doing, and if one does, it loads that skill's full body into context. You can also invoke a skill directly with /wireframe or whatever the folder is called, but the auto path is the interesting one. It's a semantic match too, not keyword, so Claude reads your message and makes a judgment call about what fits.

There's a third layer called progressive disclosure. If your skill needs more than a few hundred lines, you can split the extra material into supporting files inside the same folder and reference them from SKILL.md, and Claude only loads those when the branch that needs them fires. So compared to a stash, the routing moves off you. You describe what you want and Claude picks which one is the right fit. And there's only one canonical version of each skill in the folder now, so it tends to drift less.

I added one line to my Claude Code prompts, and the difference was night and day

One line is all it took

16
By  Mahnoor Faisal

The one decision that shapes your entire skills folder

Large skills with internal branches, or thin skills with tight descriptions

When I first started out with skills in Claude, I hit a fork in the road: one big skill with branching inside, or a bunch of small focused ones? I ended up with a mix because the pattern is more important than the specific skills. What matters most is that it saves you from rewrites a couple of months in so you're not relying on an outdated prompt stash and don't have to worry about keeping it up to date yourself.

The large skill pattern is one folder with one SKILL.md, with branches inside: "if the user asks for a wireframe, do this, if they ask for a critique, do that". This is good for when the tasks share context. My UI work all leans on the same rules, like a grayscale palette, real labels not lorem ipsum, and cross-boxes for image placeholders, so a single ui-work skill covers wireframing, critique, and layout prototyping without duplicating any of the shared bits.

The thin skill pattern is many folders, each doing one job with a tight description. This is better for when the tasks are unrelated, and also easier for Claude to route correctly because there's less overlap for it to weigh up.

The failure mode of a large skill is that a long file eats tokens on branches you're not using in a given session, which is what progressive disclosure exists to fix. Move the heavy detail into a references/ file and point at it from the main body. Thin skills can also fail but differently; usually through descriptions bleeding into each other. So being surgical matters. One skill says "low-fi wireframes with grayscale and cross-boxes" and the other says "production-ready styled components with real content", which sounds similar, but they're very different.

The thing nobody really talks about is that the description field is the entire routing layer, and most people write it like documentation. It should read like the sentence you'd actually type. If you'd say "wireframe me a login page," your description needs the word "wireframe" in it, not "generates low-fidelity structural HTML blueprints for interface planning."

Your CLAUDE.md is probably wrong, and here's how Anthropic's engineers actually structure theirs

Your file is probably doing more harm than good

By  Mahnoor Faisal

The format of a prompt library doesn't matter, the pattern does

Skills didn't teach me anything new about what I want Claude Code to do, my prompts were fine. What changed is who was doing the routing. Now I don't scroll or copy-paste anything anymore, and I'm a little annoyed at how long I waited before finally implementing Claude Skills into my workflow.

item.title: I replaced my DIY Home Assistant setup with UGREEN's all-in-one hub, and the tradeoffs surprised me
item.itunes:title: I replaced my DIY Home Assistant setup with UGREEN's all-in-one hub, and the tradeoffs surprised me
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For many smart home enthusiasts, your home automation backend lives on a custom-assembled DIY box or even a mini PC running Proxmox or bare metal Home Assistant OS. It likely works brilliantly, but maintaining a fragmented home lab stack comes with taxes like Proxmox kernel panics, dying CMOS batteries, external USB dongles hanging off of unpowered hubs, and the dreaded tangle of power bricks and cables behind your media center.

I decided to test the waters of the UGREEN Home Agent HA100, a purpose-built local AI storage and smart home control hub designed to unify device management, and it also comes with built-in neural hardware. However, moving over to this polished all-in-one appliance was a bit of a double-edged sword. It dramatically slashed power consumption, introduced hardware-accelerated local AI inference, and cleaned up physical cable clutter, but in turn, it forced me to compromise on granular kernel-level control and vendor ecosystem boundaries.

I don't need Claude, this is the local LLM I run on my NAS that powers my smart home

Qwen is what you need for your smart home

15
By  Anurag Singh

What sets this device apart?

The UGREEN HomeAgent HA100 stands out amongst DIY options

When comparing the hardware and silicon of a traditional DIY box and the UGREEN HA100, there are some stark differences. With a DIY box, whether that's an Intel NUC or a refurbished mini PC, you typically get absolute hardware freedom, raw BIOS access, multiple direct USB ports for Zigbee or Z-Wave dongles and zero proprietary software layers. Ultimately, you have complete control over your smart home and what you want it to be.

In turn, it comes with weaknesses, like, limited internal storage expansion, no native neural processing unit on a lot of models if you want to host local vision or voice models and zero built-in redundancy.

Contrast this with the UGREEN Home Agent HA100 and it feels like it's a completely different device. It comes with a turnkey design combining local storage, smart security handling, and agentic AI processing directly on local silicon. It's essentially designed specifically to bridge local automation engines with on-device intelligence, but it comes with closed proprietary bootloader/firmware layers, locked-down BIOS configurations, and potential abstraction layers between user-managed containers and the native hardware stack.

Because of its design, it can be significantly less intimidating for users who want to finally make the leap into Home Lab devices without a lot of technical barriers. However, you do lose a significant element of control, which can be fundamental for a lot of users.

The pros of making the switch

You get a range of benefits when adopting

There are some significant pros. The UGREEN Home Agent HA100 wins in a lot of areas. There are genuine engineering and operational victories when you switch over to this dedicated local AI hub. You get physical consolidation and cable cleanliness. While this isn't important to some, for others it can be fundamental when you have a messy cluster of external hardware: drive enclosures, power adapters, and mini PCs. Being able to collapse them into a single sleek tower designed for living room or utility closet placement can feel like a relief. You no longer have to hide a bundle of different devices in the back of a wardrobe. The UGREEN Home Agent HA100 can live comfortably in plain view.

You also get integrated local AI and vision pipelines. You can leverage built-in local AI acceleration for smart security object detection, local voice commands, and agentic automation, passing without routing data to an external cloud API. In order to do this as effectively on your own home lab device, you'd need to self-host the software as well as have hardware strong enough to be capable.

You also get unified storage and control. You can bridge local data storage with home automation management out of the box, eliminating the need to manually build a Frankenstein's Monster-esque setup involving a NAS plus a hypervisor. When first attempting to set up my home lab, this was what intimidated me the most. Not having to worry about connecting up a range of different home lab devices just to get my automations to run effectively feels freeing, it's already sorted out of the box.

It comes with downsides

Unfortunately, the UGREEN HomeAgent HA100 isn't one size fits all

Of course, you are making some compromises when it comes to the UGREEN Home Agent HA100. This can be particularly frustrating for a lot of power users. For example, there's a software abstraction tax. Running automations inside a vendor-managed environment introduces an essential middle layer that can complicate network bridge modes, mDNS reflection, and custom networking scripts, compared to a pure bare-metal Linux installation like you'd have on a traditional home lab mini PC or custom-built machine.

In order to run local Zigbee or Z-Wave networks, you rely on USB serial sticks on consumer appliances. Proprietary virtual machine (and, depending on your setup, container) managers sometimes complicate direct hardware device mapping after system updates. While I didn't find any issues when using the device, I can definitely see this being a problem moving forward, especially as more updates and changes roll out to the firmware.

There's always the risk of closed ecosystems in the future as well. Hardware manufacturers pushing proprietary AI assistants and unified ecosystems can occasionally lean toward walled gardens. If you have a range of different devices, you might be required to carve out workarounds to maintain open-source flexibility. While UGREEN is maintaining that this won't be an issue moving forward, there is never a 100% guarantee when you're invested in a device like this.

If you're looking for a simple and elegant entry device into home lab and automation then the UGREEN HomeAgent HA100 is just that but comes at the detriment of complete control.

Will you make the switch?

While a great device, it certainly won't be for everyone

If you're considering making the switch, I'd recommend staying DIY if you love tinkering with hypervisors, demand bare metal kernel access, and running an extensive stack of custom LXC containers. This is because you get total ownership over every line of configuration.

However, if you're just starting to get into home lab and smart home automations, then it might be better for you to invest in the UGREEN Home Agent HA100 or migrate over. If you want a clean, low-power appliance that merges local storage with native AI acceleration and smart home control, without the headache of managing a multi-device home lab stack.

While all-in-one AI hubs like the UGREEN Home Agent HA100 introduce a layer of software abstraction that purists may eye with caution, their hardware consolidation and local intelligence make them a compelling foundation for so many modern automated homes. Whether you decide to invest is totally up to you and depends on what you want out of your smart home.

item.title: 5 PC building trends we used to swear by (but don’t anymore)
item.itunes:title: 5 PC building trends we used to swear by (but don’t anymore)
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
PC building has remained fundamentally the same over the last three decades. You pick the same 8 components, assemble them into your dream build, and waste hours optimizing every little aspect of it. What has changed, however, are the underlying trends surrounding the esthetics, and the modifications we make to our rigs. From gigantic cases and custom watercooling loops to delidding and all-RGB builds, some PC building trends aren't "cool" anymore.

Full-tower cases

Stopped being popular 15 years ago

Full-tower cases used to be all the rage till the early 2010s, when people wanted tons of space for their hard drives, multiple CD-ROM drives, and elaborate cooling setups. Plus, a lot of users preferred keeping their towers on the floor, as opposed to the newer practice of keeping them on the desk, next to your monitor. Relatively compact mid-towers and mini-ITX cases are easier to keep on your desk, and are just as easy to build in.

Almost no one needs enormous cases anymore — hard drives, CD-ROM drives, and floppy drives are extinct in most setups. And complex custom watercooling loops have given way to AIO liquid coolers and air coolers. No matter how many radiators you want to install, or the number of fans you want to cram in your case, there's a mid-tower that's up to the task. Besides, mid-towers and SFF cases look sleeker and blend in better with the rest of the setup.

All-RGB builds

Ridiculous, Gaudy, Bygone

"To each their own" is something I always believe in, but excessive RGB is one of the PC trends that rapidly exploded before becoming a no-no in the last few years. From enhancing the looks of the PC to becoming the butt of jokes, RGB has been on a journey. Done tastefully, RGB lighting can still make a build look classy, but when you take it to the extreme, "rainbow puke" isn't an inaccurate summation.

Manufacturers aren't stopping, though — RGB went from components to monitors, and even on GPU support brackets. You can find RGB deskmats, heatsinks, cables, and even chairs if you want. Combined with gaudy lighting that some people like to flood their PC room with, the entire scene quickly resembles a nightclub, and not the sophisticated kind. While RGB components, devices, and accessories won't disappear anytime soon, all-RGB builds have certainly dropped in popularity.

Overclocking CPUs and GPUs

Overrated, more like

Overclocking used to be the badge of honor for builders who went the extra mile to squeeze every ounce of performance from their builds. It was almost expected to push your CPU and GPU to their realistic limits; otherwise, you were leaving performance on the table. Today, however, overclocking has stopped being relevant. The gains aren't there anymore, and PC building has gone mainstream.

Manufacturers started pushing CPUs and GPUs almost to their limits right out of the factory to target the new-age builders who prefer components that "just work." Overclocking became a niche hobby (more so than before) that yielded far too little for far too much effort. Some builders still do it on principle, but I see many more people undervolt their hardware instead of overclocking it. It reduces operating temps, extends component lifespan, and even gives you a small performance boost.

Custom loop watercooling

Much ado about nothing

  • Credit: Custom PC by Michael John Larcerna
  • Credit: Custom PC by AK Mod
  • Credit: Custom PC by Michael John Larcerna
  • Credit: Custom PC by AK Mod

While custom watercooling loops look superb, and provide cooling for not just the CPU, but multiple components simultaneously, most people just don't benefit enough from it anymore. The budget builder has no choice but to pick a $35 air cooler or $50 AIO; the mid-range builder upgrades to a better AIO or air cooler; and the high-end builder spends the extra budget on other high-end parts.

Custom loops are now relevant only to the enthusiasts of the enthusiasts — content creators or builders who can spend a ton on esthetics. A custom loop can still transform your PC visually, and even offer thermal benefits over an AIO, but the performance benefits are slim, and the cost and effort are high. Most CPUs and GPUs, even the high-end ones, can be tamed with AIOs, and it's far easier to craft a good-looking build without a custom watercooling loop.

CPU delidding

The risk-reward ratio is skewed

The only thing more complex on this list than custom watercooling is delidding your CPU. Removing the IHS to expose the CPU die for direct-die cooling (or replacing the TIM) has inherent risks. You can easily break your CPU permanently, and it obviously voids the warranty. The objective here is better thermals — something that just isn't possible without getting rid of the IHS. However, the gains aren't worth the risk.

Modern chips are comfortable running near their TJMax, the temperature beyond which the CPU starts to throttle performance. They are designed to provide the maximum performance out of the box, and if you're really chasing lower temps, you can invest in a decent cooler and undervolt your CPU. Resorting to delidding isn't for everyone, and numerous accounts on Reddit show broken CPUs as a result of incorrect delidding.

PC building doesn't need to be complicated

You don't need to make life difficult for yourself just because you're building a PC instead of buying a pre-built. Things like delidding your CPU, crafting a custom loop, or even overclocking your hardware aren't relevant anymore, at least not for most people. PC building goes through trends just like any other sphere of life, and stuff like all-RGB builds and full-tower cases stopped being popular years ago.

item.itunes:title: I disabled these hidden Pixel settings and gained a few hours of extra battery life
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When it comes to my smartphones, I want the battery to last as long as possible — especially on my Pixel devices, since Google's latest flagship smartphone is often my daily device.

Several obvious things drain my Pixel 11 Pro's battery, including cranking up the display brightness, using the always-on display, and apps that constantly ping my data connection and pull information, like social media platforms or even weather apps. In most cases, I don't want to change settings that limit what my Pixel 11 Pro can do. After all, that's the entire point of a smartphone, right?

That said, a few lesser-known features like Wi-Fi and Bluetooth Scanning can contribute to your Pixel's battery draining, and if you're like me and want to extend it as much as possible, they're worth turning off, though there are trade-offs.

Wi-Fi Scanning eats up more battery life than you might think

Map apps might be slightly less accurate, though

On the surface, Wi-Fi Scanning seems pretty basic. You definitely want your phone to search for Wi-Fi networks, right? Otherwise, how would it connect to a nearby network? Well, that's not actually what this feature does (turning on Wi-Fi scans for Wi-Fi networks already). Wi-Fi scanning happens all the time, including even when Wi-Fi scanning is off.

Here's how it works: when your Pixel detects a network, it uses it for location services. This helps apps that require your location, like Google Maps or Uber, figure out where you are more accurately if you're indoors and your GPS reception is poor. At the same time, Wi-Fi Scanning can also hurt battery life, since apps can use it to improve that location accuracy.

To turn off Wi-Fi scanning on my Pixel 11 Pro, I head to Settings > Location > Location Services > Wi-Fi scanning. You'll still be able to find Wi-Fi networks like normal, and map apps will continue to track your location using only GPS. However, they'll likely be a bit less accurate at indicating your location.

3 simple settings I changed to stop my Pixel from overheating

Changing this simple setting keeps my Pixel chilled out

By  Patrick O'Rourke

Bluetooth Scanning also improves GPS location accuracy

Turning off Bluetooth Scanning can help save battery life

Along with Wi-Fi Scanning, Pixel devices also use Bluetooth Scanning to improve location accuracy. In this case, Bluetooth scanning uses nearby devices to gather information about where you are, then passes it to apps. Like Wi-Fi scanning, Bluetooth Scanning runs constantly in the background, regardless of whether Bluetooth is on or off.

This means the feature constantly wakes up your phone's Bluetooth sensor. While Bluetooth doesn't consume as much power as Wi-Fi, it still uses a fair amount of battery. Plus, disabling both Wi-Fi Scanning and Bluetooth Scanning helps you save even more juice. To turn off Bluetooth scanning, head to Settings > Location > Location services > Bluetooth scanning.

Turning off both features won't really break anything

You might not even notice a difference

While both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth Scanning offer more accurate location data to apps, especially when it comes to apps that need to pinpoint your location, depending on what apps you use on your phone, you might not even notice much of a performance difference. At the same time, there's a trade-off, especially since GPS likely isn't as precise as some people assume. You might run into a situation where Google Maps takes a few more seconds to locate you, or the Uber app can't precisely place your pick-up spot.

It's tough to put a number on how much battery life turning features like this off can save, but it won't give you a massive boost. At the same time, 5-10% isn't insignificant either, especially if you don't charge your Pixel device very often. Of course, the battery-life benefits you'll get from turning off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth scanning will depend on other factors, including which apps you use most often and other key settings like display brightness and background app usage.

Still, if you're looking to save a bit of extra battery life, turning off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth Scanning is a solid option.
